function.name: calculate_electric_current
function.description: Calculate the electric current through a conductor given voltage and resistance. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

voltage.description: The voltage across the conductor in Volts. This is a float type value.

resistance.description: The resistance of the conductor in Ohms. This is a float type value.

conductance.description: The conductance of the conductor in Siemens. Optional if resistance is provided. Default: 0.3 This is a float type value.

message.content:
Electricity wasn’t “discovered” by a single individual—rather it emerged from a long chain of observations and experiments carried out by many thinkers over several centuries: | Era | Key figure(s) | Contribution | |-----|---------------|--------------| | **Ancient Greece** | *Thales of Miletus* (~600 BCE) | Noted static attraction when rubbing amber (“electrum”). | | **16th‑17th Century** | *William Gilbert* (1544–1603) | Published _De Magnete_ (1600), distinguishing magnetism from electrostatics and coining the word “electric.” | | **Late 1700s – Early 1800s** | *Benjamin Franklin*, *Alessandro Volta*, *Luigi Galvani*, *Hans Christian Ørsted* | • Franklin’s kite experiment (1752) linked lightning to electricity.
• Volta invented the voltaic pile (first battery).
• Galvani studied bioelectric phenomena ("animal electricity").
• Ørsted found that electric currents produce magnetic fields (1820). | | **Mid‑19th Century** | *Michael Faraday*, *James Clerk Maxwell* | Faraday formulated electromagnetic induction (1831); Maxwell unified electromagnetism into four equations (1865). | So while early Greek philosophers noticed electrical effects, modern scientific understanding—and what we think of today as “discovering electricity”—was built incrementally by scholars such as William Gilbert, Benjamin Franklin, Alessandro Volta, Hans Christian Ørsted, Michael Faraday, and James Clerk Maxwell.
